title: Brain Abscess
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: A brain abscess is a focal intracerebral infection that forms a pus‑filled cavity. It usually follows spread from ear, sinus, dental, or hematogenous sources, and its microbiology reflects the portal of entry and local epidemiology.

sections.p: Brain abscess is a space‑occupying lesion of the brain parenchyma containing purulent material, surrounded by a capsule after 1–2 weeks. It presents with fever, headache, and focal neurological deficits, and can rapidly become life‑threatening if the capsule ruptures.
b: Incidence 0.3–1.3 per 100 000 per year worldwide
Common in low‑resource settings due to untreated otitis media, sinusitis, dental infections, and HIV/TB

sections.p: The causative flora is polymicrobial in most cases. Anaerobes dominate when the source is oral or sinus; streptococci, staphylococci, and gram‑negative bacilli are frequent in otogenic and hematogenous spread. In immunocompromised patients, fungi (Aspergillus) and Nocardia are important.
b: Anaerobic streptococci (e.g., *Streptococcus milleri* group)
Aerobic streptococci (*S. aureus*, *S. pneumoniae*)
Gram‑negative bacilli (*Klebsiella*, *Pseudomonas*)
Fungi (*Aspergillus*, *Candida*) in HIV/TB patients

sections.p: Pathogens reach the brain by three routes: direct extension from contiguous infections (ear, sinus, mastoid, dental), hematogenous spread from distant foci (lung abscess, endocarditis, septicemia), and trauma or neurosurgery.
b: Contiguous spread – most common in low‑resource settings
Hematogenous spread – often from lung abscess, endocarditis, or TB meningitis
Post‑traumatic or post‑operative inoculation

sections.p: The infection evolves through four stages: early cerebritis, late cerebritis, early capsule formation, and mature capsule. Clinical severity depends on size, location, and host immunity.
b: Early cerebritis (days 1‑3): diffuse inflammation, no capsule
Late cerebritis (days 4‑9): necrosis, beginning capsule
Early capsule (days 10‑13): well‑defined ring, mass effect
Mature capsule (>2 weeks): thick wall, possible rupture

sections.p: Imaging is the cornerstone; CT with contrast shows a ring‑enhancing lesion, MRI is more sensitive. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated unless the diagnosis is uncertain and imaging is unavailable.

t.b: Confirms presence, size, location, and mass effect of an abscess; ring enhancement suggests capsule
Distinguishes abscess (restricted diffusion) from tumor or necrotic infarct
Detect systemic inflammation; high CRP supports infection
Provides microbiology for targeted therapy and reduces mass effect

sections.p: Management combines antimicrobial therapy, surgical drainage when feasible, and control of intracranial pressure. Choice of antibiotics reflects the most likely organisms and local resistance patterns.
b: Empiric IV regimen: ceftriaxone + metronidazole ± vancomycin (covers streptococci, anaerobes, MRSA).
Add antifungal (e.g., voriconazole) if immunocompromised and fungal risk high.
Avoid aminoglycosides alone – poor CNS penetration.
Surgical drainage (stereotactic aspiration or craniotomy) for lesions >2.5 cm, mass effect, or neurologic decline.
If surgery unavailable, extend IV antibiotics 6–8 weeks and monitor with repeat imaging.

sections.p: Focus on the clinical reasoning chain: source identification, imaging, microbiology, and timely drainage.
b: Never perform lumbar puncture when a mass lesion is suspected.
Ring‑enhancing lesion in a patient with chronic otitis media → think otogenic abscess.
Rapid neurologic decline → urgent neurosurgical decompression.
In HIV/TB endemic area, consider *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* or fungal causes.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of consciousness, new seizures, or signs of herniation (bilateral pupil dilation, decerebrate posturing)
Rapidly worsening focal deficit or increasing headache despite antibiotics

faq.a: Because the pressure from the abscess can cause brain herniation when CSF is removed.

faq.q: What is the most common source of brain abscess in East Africa?
faq.a: Chronic otitis media and sinusitis, often with anaerobic oral flora.
For lesions >2.5 cm, causing mass effect, or when neurologic status deteriorates.

exam: What immediate step would you take for a patient with fever, focal deficit, and a ring‑enhancing lesion on CT? — Obtain neurosurgical opinion for possible drainage and start empiric IV antibiotics.

How does the microbiology differ between an otogenic and a hematogenous brain abscess? — Otogenic: anaerobes and streptococci; hematogenous: staphylococci, gram‑negative bacilli, or TB/fungi in immunocompromised.
Why is metronidazole included in the empiric regimen? — It provides excellent anaerobic coverage, crucial for oral and sinus sources.
A patient on antitubercular therapy develops a new brain lesion; what should you consider? — Tuberculous brain abscess or paradoxical TB meningitis; adjust regimen and add steroids if needed.
What imaging feature helps differentiate an abscess from a high‑grade tumor? — Restricted diffusion on DWI MRI and a thin, uniform ring enhancement.
If neurosurgical facilities are unavailable, how do you manage a 3 cm abscess? — Prolonged high‑dose IV antibiotics (6–8 weeks) with close clinical and repeat CT monitoring.
Which host factor most increases mortality in brain abscess? — HIV infection or severe immunosuppression, because of atypical organisms and poor response.
Explain why aminoglycosides are avoided in brain abscess therapy. — They have poor penetration of the blood‑brain barrier and can cause nephro‑/ototoxicity without added benefit.
